actions.justification: Mandatory first step - assess HR, BP, SpO2, RR for hemodynamic stability and to identify signs of massive PE (hypotension, hypoxia, tachycardia).
Mandatory - Wells score stratifies pre-test probability for PE in this patient presenting with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain, guiding diagnostic pathway (D-dimer vs. direct CTPA).
Mandatory - D-dimer is the key initial biomarker for PE workup; a negative result in low/intermediate probability effectively rules out PE without need for imaging.

A 12-lead ECG is a Class I recommendation for acute chest pain to evaluate for STEMI or right heart strain patterns (S1Q3T3) consistent with PE, and should be obtained within 10 minutes of presentation per AHA guidelines.
Patient presenting with acute dyspnea warrants supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO2 and support tissue oxygenation while diagnostic workup proceeds, even with current SpO2 of 98%.

Chest X-ray is indicated per AHA chest pain guidelines to evaluate alternative diagnoses. In this patient with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain (suspected PE), CXR helps rule out pneumothorax, pneumonia, or other causes and is part of the standard initial workup.

Echocardiogram can assess for right heart strain, which is an important finding in pulmonary embolism and helps with risk stratification (massive vs submassive PE). Given the presentation of acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain with Wells score already assessed, echo provides key hemodynamic information.

A 12-lead ECG is indicated per AHA guidelines for acute chest pain to evaluate for STEMI and other cardiac etiologies. Note: order_ecg was already done but order_imaging_ecg is a distinct available action and should be completed to ensure full ECG workup is captured in this phase.

Given the clinical presentation of acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain with elevated Wells score concern for pulmonary embolism, CT pulmonary angiography is the gold-standard imaging test to confirm or exclude PE. This is the next critical diagnostic step after D-dimer and chest X-ray have been ordered.
Pulmonology consultation is appropriate given the presentation of acute dyspnea with pleuritic chest pain and suspected PE to assist with further management planning.
Arterial blood gas will assess oxygenation, ventilation, and A-a gradient, which is important in PE evaluation even with normal SpO2, as it can reveal hypoxemia or hypocapnia consistent with PE.
Lower extremity venous Doppler ultrasound can identify DVT as the source of potential pulmonary embolism, supporting diagnosis and guiding anticoagulation decisions.
Echocardiogram (bedside/TTE) can assess for right ventricular strain or dilation, which is important for risk stratification of PE severity and hemodynamic impact.

CBC is indicated to evaluate for infection, anemia, or other hematologic abnormalities that may contribute to or complicate the presentation of suspected PE with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain.
BNP helps assess right ventricular strain, which is important for risk stratification in suspected pulmonary embolism and guides management decisions.
BMP provides baseline renal function (critical before contrast CT-PA results are reviewed and before initiating anticoagulation), electrolytes, and metabolic status.

Troponin is indicated to assess for right heart strain/myocardial injury in suspected PE, and has not yet been ordered. Elevated troponin would indicate higher risk and influence management decisions.
Coagulation studies (PT/INR, aPTT) are needed prior to anticoagulation therapy to establish baseline and guide dosing, and have not yet been completed.
Lactate helps assess tissue perfusion and hemodynamic compromise in suspected PE, which can stratify risk (submassive vs massive PE) and guide treatment intensity.

Patient presents with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain, with extensive workup already completed including CT-PA ordered. Given high clinical suspicion for pulmonary embolism (Wells score assessed, D-dimer ordered, CT-PA ordered), empiric anticoagulation is appropriate while awaiting confirmatory imaging results, provided no contraindications exist. This aligns with PE management guidelines recommending anticoagulation initiation when clinical probability is high.

Patient presents with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain, highly suggestive of pulmonary embolism. Extensive workup including CT-PA, D-dimer, Wells score, and coagulation studies have been ordered. Patient is hemodynamically stable (HR 80, BP 120/80, SpO2 98%). LMWH anticoagulation is the standard initial treatment for suspected/confirmed PE in stable patients per PE management guidelines, while awaiting confirmatory imaging results.

In the context of possible pulmonary embolism with right heart strain, cautious IV fluid administration can help maintain preload and hemodynamic stability, particularly while awaiting definitive diagnosis and in anticipation of potential right ventricular strain identified on echocardiogram.

Patient presents with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain consistent with pulmonary embolism. While LMWH has been given, transitioning to or supplementing with unfractionated heparin (UFH) may be indicated especially if CT-PA confirms PE and the patient may need procedural intervention. UFH provides more titratable anticoagulation and is preferred if thrombolysis or catheter-directed therapy is being considered.

Patient has acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain with CT-PA already ordered, suggesting possible PE workup. Interventional radiology consult is appropriate for potential catheter-directed therapy or IVC filter placement if massive/submassive PE is confirmed, given anticoagulation has already been initiated.
